prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [val] Code · CLI flags (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Flag" · longest unbreakable word 106px · one-line width 204px
  col 2: header "Type" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 55px
  col 3: header "Default" · longest unbreakable word 114px · one-line width 114px
  col 4: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 89px · one-line width 477px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 625px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 624px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The descriptions are readable, but two flag names wrap, making the commands harder to scan and copy."},"B":{"grade":"excellent","why":"All flags and defaults stay on one line, while the descriptions wrap into manageable phrases and the rows remain easy to compare."},"C":{"grade":"bad","why":"Equal column widths waste space on short types and defaults, leaving both flags and descriptions cramped; several flags split and descriptions become tall."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The generous description column reads well, but three flag names split across lines despite unused space in the default column."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Flags and defaults stay intact, but the narrower description column produces an extra line in the first row and a taller table than B."},"F":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Descriptions have comfortable space, but two flag names wrap while the default column has room to spare."}},"best":["B"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"The relative importance of compact descriptions versus keeping flag names on one line depends on the table’s intended use; for a CLI reference, intact flags are especially valuable."}
